       1   Q      HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY PROVIDED TESTIMONY TO THE OKLAHOMA

       2          CORPORATION COMMISSION ("OCC" OR "COMMISSION")?

       3   A      Yes.   I have previously provided testimony to the Commission in Case Nos. PUD

       4          2015-00273, 2017-00261, 2018-00084, and 2021-00172.


       5   Q      HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY PROVIDED TESTIMONY TO STATE ELECTRIC UTILITY

       6          REGULATORY COMMISSIONS WITH RESPECT TO LARGE LOAD ADDITIONS?

       7   A      Yes, I have done so in Illinois Commerce Commission Docket Nos. 25-0677 and

       8          25-0679, Louisiana Public Service Commission Docket Nos. U-37425 and U-37882,

       9          and Michigan Public Service Commission Case Nos. U-21859, U-21986, U-22058 and

      10          U-22061.



      11   Q      ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

      12   A      This testimony is presented on behalf of Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers

      13          ("OIEC"). OlEC is an unincorporated association consisting of a diverse group of large

      14          consumers of energy involved in Oklahoma regulatory and legislative matters primarily

      15          involving the supply of natural gas and electric power to large consumers of energy.



      16   Q      WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?

      17   A      My testimony will address the Extra Large Power and Light ("XLPL") Tariff and Terms

      18          and Conditions of Service for Extra Large Load Customers ("T&CXLLC") proposed by

      19          Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company ("OG&E" or "Company") in this proceeding as

      20          well as OG&E’s proposal to defer the costs associated with the implementation of

      21          portfolio optimization modeling software.

       1                  My silence with regard to any position taken by OG&E in its application or direct

       2          testimony in this proceeding does not indicate my endorsement of that position



       3   Q      PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR CONCLUSIONS.

       4   A      Based on my review and analysis of OG&E's direct testimony, OG&E's response to

       5          data requests in this proceeding, and the Oklahoma Data Center Customer Ratepayer

       6          Protection Act of 2026 (17 O.S. §§ 901-905) ("HB 2992") and applying my knowledge

       7          and experience, I have concluded the following:

       8              •   OG&E's proposed applicability of its XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC is
       9                  inconsistent with, and goes well beyond, what is required by HB 2992.
      10                  Contrary to the Large Load Customer definition of HB 2992, OG&E
      11                  proposes to apply the XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC to: (i) the commercial,
      12                  agricultural and industrial ratepayers the Oklahoma Legislature expressly
      13                  excluded from that definition; (ii) any increase in demand, no matter how
      14                  small, that causes an existing customer's total demand to reach 125 MW;
      15                  (iii) existing customers that add no load at all ("Customer Type 3"); and
      16                  (iv) the entirety of an existing customer's load rather than only the portion of
      17                  its load added after July 1, 2026.

      18              •   OG&E has not reasonably justified its departure from HB 2992. The only
      19                  justification OG&E has offered is a two-sentence discovery response that is
      20                  not supported by analysis and is contradicted by OG&E's own presentation
      21                  of this case, which is grounded in the unique risks of serving data center
      22                  loads. The elevated stranded cost risk that motivates protections of this
      23                  kind is characteristic of computational loads, not of traditional commercial,
      24                  agricultural and industrial loads, and the focus of HB 2992 on computational
      25                  loads is consistent with the approach of NERC and pending federal
      26                  legislation. Furthermore, the customers OG&E has specifically publicly
      27                  identified in discovery are all data centers, cryptocurrency mining operations
      28                  or artificial-intelligence computing facilities that are already captured by the
      29                  HB 2992 definition, so conforming the applicability of the XLPL Tariff and
      30                  T&CXLLC to HB 2992 would not deprive OG&E or its other customers of
      31                  any needed protection.

      32              •   OG&E's proposed Customer Affordability Charge and Reservation Charge
      33                  are not based on cost causation principles as required by HB 2992. The
      34                  Customer Affordability Charge was simply designed to produce
      35                  approximately $30 million from 1,000 MW of XLPL Tariff customer demand
      36                  sized to an amount large enough to fund existing residential assistance,
      37                  senior discount and energy efficiency programs, none of which are costs

       1                  incurred to serve XLPL Tariff customers; the Reservation Charge is not
       2                  based on any identified or estimated pre-service cost; and the revenues
       3                  from both charges would be credited exclusively to the residential customer
       4                  class, which is unduly discriminatory toward OG&E’s other customer
       5                  classes. Neither charge is analogous to a system contribution charge, which
       6                  is used in conjunction with incremental cost-based economic development
       7                  rates and benefits all customer classes.

       8              •   OG&E’s proposed CIAC requirement is reasonable for distribution facilities,
       9                  transmission facilities that solely serve the XLPL Tariff customer and
      10                  transmission upgrades whose costs are directly assigned to OG&E by
      11                  Southwest Power Pool ("SPP").         However, it is not reasonable for
      12                  transmission network upgrades whose costs are rolled into SPP
      13                  transmission rates and OG&E retail rates because, although those
      14                  upgrades would not be needed but for the XLPL Tariff customer's load
      15                  addition, they serve OG&E's customers as a whole. OG&E's incremental
      16                  revenue requirement for such network upgrades should instead be
      17                  accounted for in the process to determine the Customer Class Protection
      18                  Charge.

      19              •   OG&E's proposed Minimum Billing Energy provision, which is based on a
      20                  90% load factor applied to Billing Demand, is not supported by any analysis
      21                  by any OG&E witness. It would apply to base rate energy charges and rider
      22                  energy charges that provide for recovery of costs that are in large part either
      23                  not incrementally affected by service to XLPL Tariff customers or only
      24                  incrementally affected in proportion to actual energy consumption by XLPL
      25                  Tariff customers, thereby causing the provision to act more as a guaranteed
      26                  contribution toward existing OG&E costs than as stranded cost protection;
      27                  OG&E has not demonstrated the provision is needed on top of the proposed
      28                  85% Minimum Billing Demand and the Customer Class Protection Charge;
      29                  and the 90% load factor would likely be well in excess of the actual load
      30                  factor of some customers subject to the XLPL Tariff. In addition, the use of
      31                  a minimum billing energy provision for stranded cost protection is rare and,
      32                  in the one other instance I am aware of, it was set at a much lower 65% load
      33                  factor.

      34              •   While the concept of comparing class cost of service studies with and
      35                  without the XLPL Tariff class is sound, OG&E's proposed process to
      36                  determine the Customer Class Protection Charge is deficient in two
      37                  respects. First, it fails to address how the incremental production resource
      38                  costs and incremental transmission network upgrade costs (not covered by
      39                  CIAC payments or other direct assignment) that OG&E would not have
      40                  incurred but for XLPL Tariff load additions will be treated in the two studies;
      41                  those costs must be included only in the study that includes the XLPL Tariff
      42                  class. Second, because the Minimum Billing Demand and Minimum Billing
      43                  Energy percentages were not set based on OG&E's incremental cost to
      44                  serve XLPL Tariff customers, the process needs, but lacks, a mechanism
      45                  to lower the XLPL Tariff Service Level 1 and Service Level 2 Capacity

       1                  Demand Charges if the study results show the XLPL Tariff class is
       2                  subsidizing OG&E's other customer classes.

       3              •   OG&E's proposed 15-year fully ramped minimum initial term is 50% longer
       4                  than the at least 10-year term required by HB 2992, and OG&E has provided
       5                  no analysis in its direct testimony or in discovery to justify that extension.
       6                  OG&E witness DeCourcey's own comparison shows minimum terms of 8 to
       7                  12 years at more than half of the utilities he reviewed. A 15-year minimum
       8                  initial term is not necessary to protect OG&E's existing customers from
       9                  stranded cost risk if the termination and capacity reduction fees are properly
      10                  designed.

      11              •   OG&E's proposed termination and capacity reduction fees are not properly
      12                  designed to protect OG&E's existing customers. Because they are based
      13                  on the Minimum Charges for the remainder of the initial term rather than on
      14                  the remaining net plant of the incremental production resource investments
      15                  and transmission network upgrades made to serve the customer less the
      16                  residual value of those investments to OG&E's other customers, they could
      17                  substantially overstate or understate actual stranded costs. Furthermore,
      18                  no fee at all would apply to a customer that exits at the end of the initial term
      19                  even though the depreciable lives of those investments will generally be well
      20                  in excess of 15 years. A fee based on remaining net plant less residual
      21                  value, applied whenever a customer terminates or reduces service, would
      22                  make the fee exactly equal to the stranded costs at issue and would fully
      23                  support a 10-year fully ramped minimum initial term.

      24              •   The XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC provide no means for an XLPL Tariff
      25                  customer that is willing and able to have its load interrupted to take
      26                  interruptible service, even though doing so could significantly reduce the
      27                  incremental production investment OG&E would need to make to serve the
      28                  customer. The current uncertainty regarding SPP's load modifier provisions
      29                  is a temporary matter that does not justify the absence of any interruptible
      30                  service option.

      31              •   The XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC provide no defined option for an XLPL Tariff
      32                  customer to voluntarily purchase renewable and other clean power above
      33                  the level inherently provided under standard service, which many entities
      34                  require to meet their corporate sustainability requirements or goals.
      35                  OG&E's stated intent to address this on a "case-by-case basis" is not an
      36                  adequate substitute for a defined tariff option.

      37              •   Neither the XLPL Tariff nor the T&CXLLC contains any provision that would
      38                  allow an XLPL Tariff customer to supply some or all of its generation needs
      39                  pursuant to a BYOG or other wholesale power or self-supply arrangement.
      40                  A properly structured BYOG program would alleviate the need for OG&E to
      41                  acquire new production resources to serve the customer and eliminate
      42                  production-related stranded cost risk for OG&E's existing customers, and
      43                  therefore warrants consideration by the Commission.

       1              •   OG&E does not intend to file individual XLPL Tariff customer ESAs with the
       2                  Commission or otherwise offer them for review by the PUD Staff or
       3                  intervenors. Given the potentially enormous size of XLPL Tariff load
       4                  additions and the significant discretion OG&E has reserved to itself to
       5                  deviate from the XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC in individual ESAs, PUD Staff
       6                  and intervenor review of each executed ESA, with the opportunity to seek
       7                  Commission review, is warranted.

       8              •   Neither OG&E's direct testimony nor its proposed XLPL Tariff and
       9                  T&CXLLC requires OG&E to demonstrate, for each XLPL Tariff load
      10                  addition, that it has sufficient existing and planned generation resources to
      11                  serve that load addition and its existing customers while maintaining
      12                  resource adequacy. To the contrary, the standard form ESA contemplates
      13                  the procurement of interim capacity such that OG&E could commit to serve
      14                  a new XLPL Tariff load addition without any demonstration that it can
      15                  reliably do so.

      16              •   Neither the XLPL Tariff nor the T&CXLLC provides OG&E any ability to
      17                  delay the load ramp of an XLPL Tariff customer in the event the in-service
      18                  date of the production resource additions necessary to serve that customer
      19                  is delayed, and the Force Majeure provision of the standard form ESA
      20                  expressly excludes vendor and supplier delays. Because a delay in those
      21                  resource additions could seriously threaten resource adequacy for OG&E's
      22                  existing customers, this is a critical omission.

      23              •   Although OIEC supports OG&E acquiring and utilizing portfolio optimization
      24                  modeling software in its resource planning and RFP analyses, the
      25                  acquisition and use of such software is part of the normal course of business
      26                  for an electric utility of OG&E's size and does not warrant the special cost
      27                  recovery treatment of a regulatory asset. Granting cost deferral would also
      28                  fail to consider whether OG&E has offsetting decreases in cost or increases
      29                  in revenue that partially or fully eliminate any need for deferral.



      30   Q      PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR RECOMMENDATIONS.

      31   A       recommend that the Commission reject OG&E's proposed XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC

      32          as filed and to condition any approval it provides of the proposed XLPL Tariff and

      33          T&CXLLC on OG&E making a compliance filing that:

      34              1. Changes the definition of "Customer" in the T&CXLLC, as detailed of the
      35                 body of my testimony herein, such that it fully conforms to the definition of
      36                 Large Load Customer under HB 2992 and clearly excludes all residential,
      37                 commercial, agricultural or industrial ratepayers.

       2                  strikes subpart (ii) regarding increases in customer demand that cause the
       3                  customer's total demand to be 125 MW or more.

       4               3. Eliminates "Customer Type 3" from the T&CXLLC and the XLPL Tariff.

      26          schedule and accompanying T&CXLLC that would govern retail electric service to Extra

      27          Large Load Customers effective July 1, 2026.4 Under OG&E's proposal, three types

      28          of customers would be required to take service under the XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC:

           provisions.

           Commissioning, Operations, Protection, and Control, which outlined seven actions registered entities must
           implement to address immediate risks posed by computational loads interfacing with the BPS. The Level 3 alert was
           issued as NERC observed customer-initiated large load reductions and significant oscillations that occur in seconds,
           leaving little or no room for real-time responses and posing a threat to BPS reliability. The deadline for registered
           entities to submit their responses is August 3, 2026.

           actions for traditional utilities and grid operators, and the companies behind these emerging large loads
           including equipment manufacturers. The goal is to ensure that as more industrial-scale consumers connect to the
           grid, they actively participate in practices that protect grid stability. These steps highlight that proactive
           planning and participation can enable even more of these facilities to come online reliably and quickly. Although
           non-binding, NERC strongly urges all relevant entities to adopt the recommended risk mitigation strategies
           outlined in the Reliability Guideline.

            Monthly Billing Demand

            The billing demand in kW shall be taken each month as the single highest 15-minute integrated peak in kW as
            registered during the month by a demand meter or indicator, subject to off-peak hour provision but the monthly
            billing demand so established shall, in no event, be less than 90% of the greater of (a) the customer's contract
            capacity, or (b) the customer’s highest previously established monthly billing demand during the past 11
            months.

            Minimum Charge

            Large Load Customers are subject to a minimum monthly charge for each plant egualto the sum of (a) the
            Monthly Service Charge; (b) the product of the Demand Charges and the Monthly Billing Demand: (c) the
            product of the Base Power Supply Non-Capacity Energy Charge and the Base Billing Energy; (d) the sum of
            the product of each demand charge in all applicable demand related riders in effect at the time and the Monthly
            Billing Demand; and (e) the sum of the product of the Base Billing Energy and the energy charge in all
            applicable energy related riders in effect at the time. The Base Billing Energy will be computed as follows:
            Contract Capacity (kW) multiplied by 65% multiplied by Number of Billing Hours in the Month.

            is requested by the Customer the Customer is required to provide a Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC)

            Interconnection

            One or more interconnection studies may be required by the Company prior to interconnection of a new facility
            or expansion of an existing facility. Such interconnection studies are not limited to but may include a screening

            could be used to more finitely define upgrade costs for interconnection if needed. Each type of study required
            will include invoicing per an interconnection fee schedule.

            Each type of study will be the subject of a written study agreement between the Customer and the Company
            that includes the following:

                     a. A target date for completion of any required study: and

                     b. A provision to share the results of the study with the Customer and/or its representative: and

                     c. An explanation of all estimated charges to complete the interconnection after the completion of the
                     study(ies) or explanation of what further study may be needed: and

                     d. A good faith estimate of the total number of hours needed to complete the study: and

                     e. An estimate of the total interconnection study fee that will be commensurate with the total load
                     amount and complexity of the requested interconnection service.

            the Customer also demonstrates:

                     a Evidence that they possess ownership rights to the property, and
                     b. Written confirmation from the zoning authority that the required zoning is approved and
                     c. An overall site plan that includes a one-line electrical diagram.

            current amount held. A Large Load Customer with both (a) a credit rating of at least A-from S&P and A3 from
